subject: chemistry
question_text: Give the differences between σ and π bonds.

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. The book asks this SAME comparison at two lengths: VSAQ 5 (a two-row table: formation and strength) and SAQ 5 (a four-point list), so this file carries both as cuts of one answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The one-mark-per-difference splits are CLAIMS until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them; the question itself is sourced, not invented.

insider_note: The book asks this twice — a two-mark table and a four-mark list. Always write differences in matched pairs: one sentence for σ, one for π, on the same point.

cuts.label: 4-mark answer
cuts.note: Four differences, one mark each, is a claim until a teacher confirms the split.

cuts.label: 2-mark answer
cuts.note: The book's VSAQ table prints exactly these two rows: formation and strength.

steps.label: Formation
lines: 1. Formation:
σ bond — formed by axial (end-to-end)
overlap of orbitals along the internuclear
axis.
π bond — formed by sidewise (lateral)
overlap of orbitals, perpendicular to the
internuclear axis.
steps.why: The direction of overlap is the definition of each bond type, so every other difference follows from this row.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two: axial belongs to σ, sidewise belongs to π.
Writing overlap without naming the direction. The direction IS the difference.
steps.memory_tip: σ is straight along the axis; π overlaps from the side.
steps.margin_note: Write this pair first in both the 2-mark and the 4-mark form.

steps.label: Independent existence
lines: 2. Existence:
σ bond — can exist independently; it is
the first bond formed between two atoms.
π bond — cannot exist alone; it forms
only after a σ bond already exists.
steps.why: Sidewise overlap is only possible once the atoms are already held together by an axial bond, so a π bond is always the second or third bond.
common_mistakes: Saying a π bond can form on its own. It never does; the σ bond comes first.
steps.memory_tip: In any double or triple bond, bond number one is always the σ bond.
steps.margin_note: One pair of sentences. The word independently carries the point.

steps.label: Orbitals used
lines: 3. Orbitals used:
σ bond — formed by pure orbitals or by
hybrid orbitals.
π bond — formed only by pure p (or d)
orbitals, never by hybrid orbitals.
steps.why: Hybrid orbitals point along bond directions, so they can only overlap axially. The sidewise overlap of a π bond needs an unhybridised p orbital standing perpendicular to the axis.
common_mistakes: Writing that π bonds use hybrid orbitals. Hybrid orbitals give σ bonds only.
steps.memory_tip: Hybrid orbitals make σ bonds only. π bonds keep to pure p orbitals.
steps.margin_note: This is the row that links this answer to the hybridisation questions.

steps.label: Strength
lines: 4. Strength:

lines.text: σ bond is stronger than π bond

lines: The extent of overlap is greater in axial
overlap than in sidewise overlap, so the
σ bond is the stronger of the two.
steps.why: Bond strength follows the extent of orbital overlap. Axial overlap brings the orbitals together more fully than sidewise overlap does, so σ is stronger.
common_mistakes: Stating which is stronger without the reason. The extent-of-overlap sentence is part of the mark.
Writing that π is stronger because it comes in double bonds. The double bond is strong because it has TWO bonds, not because π is strong.
steps.memory_tip: More overlap means a stronger bond, and axial overlap is the fuller overlap.
steps.margin_note: Box the comparison, then give the extent-of-overlap reason under it.
